The AIDS epidemic in Africa is the spread of HIV, the virus that causes AIDS (acquired immune deficiency syndrome), across sub-Saharan Africa, which has suffered most of the world's AIDS deaths. AIDS was first recognised as a disease in the United States in 1981, but the virus came from Central Africa.

The main strain crossed from chimpanzees to humans in southern Cameroon in the early 1900s, probably through hunting. Genetic studies trace its first big spread to Kinshasa around 1920. Railways, river boats and the fast-growing colonial city carried it further. It reached Haiti and then the Americas by the 1960s.

In the 1980s and 1990s it spread along truck routes and through the migrant labour that tied mines and cities to villages. East Africa was hit first, then southern Africa worst of all. In Botswana, South Africa, Zimbabwe and Eswatini, more than a fifth of adults were infected at the peak, and life expectancy fell by more than ten years in some countries. Millions of children lost parents.

Responses differed. Uganda cut infection rates early with open public campaigns. In South Africa President Thabo Mbeki questioned the link between HIV and AIDS and delayed treatment, a choice later blamed for hundreds of thousands of deaths.

Antiretroviral drugs arrived in 1996, but they were too expensive for most Africans until cheap generic versions appeared. From the early 2000s the Global Fund and the American PEPFAR programme paid to treat millions, and deaths fell sharply. The region still has about two thirds of all people living with HIV. It is one of the defining crises of the independent African states.
